meta.label: Game consoles
meta.attribution: Options are current console models sold in the US, UK and EU: home consoles, hybrid and handheld consoles including PC handhelds, plus small-maker handhelds sold worldwide. VR headsets are left out because they are a separate decision on the map. Repairable: iFixit's handheld console repairability table or device page score (0 to 10, converted to 0 to 100). iFixit does not yet score home consoles under its current rubric, so for PlayStation and Xbox models without a score the number reflects iFixit's teardown findings and whether the maker sells genuine parts (iFixit sells genuine Microsoft parts for the Series S; Sony and Nintendo sell none); for the Steam Machine and Analogue Pocket it reflects the maker's published repair guides or battery service. Each cell says which. Back catalogue and future: what the maker says the console plays from earlier generations, and whether games bought now carry forward. Games you keep: physical media that holds the full game, the platform's licence terms, and whether games can come from outside the maker's store. First-year cost: the maker's own US store price on the date checked plus the cheapest paid membership the maker sells for online multiplayer (PlayStation Plus Essential $79.99 a year, Game Pass Essential $9.99 a month, Nintendo Switch Online $19.99 a year; Steam and Windows PCs add none), scored as 100 minus one point per $12, floor 5. Several prices rose sharply in 2026 with memory costs. Not scored: game quality and exclusives, and privacy, because every platform account is governed by the same few company-wide policies. Sources: ifixit.com, playstation.com, xbox.com, microsoft.com, nintendo.com, steampowered.com, steamdeck.com, asus.com, goretroid.com, play.date, analogue.co. Handheld consoles are included here, although the map also has a separate handheld-consoles decision; they are compared here alongside home and hybrid consoles rather than moved. Reviewed 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare game consoles by repairability, ownership, support life, and cost.

axes.label: Cost or overall fit
axes.question: Lower cost or a stronger overall fit?

axes.label: Ownership or catalogue
axes.question: Games you physically own, or the largest back catalogue?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

products.name: PlayStation 5 (disc, 1TB)
products.description: Sony's current PS5 with a Blu-ray drive, playing nearly all PS4 games, from a maker that says new games go digital-only from 2028.

repairability.note: iFixit gave the original 2020 PS5 7 out of 10 but, as it says, does not yet score home consoles under its current rubric. Its device page for the slim model group lists replacement guides for covers, disc drive, fan and power supply; its 2023 teardown praised tool-free panels, a swappable disc drive and a standard M.2 slot, but noted the drive is paired to the board online and Sony provides no parts or manuals.

longevity.note: Sony's support page says the PS5 plays 'the overwhelming majority of the 4,000+ PS4 games', but PS5 consoles do not support PlayStation 3 discs.

ownership.note: The disc model plays PS5 and PS4 discs, which can be lent or resold. But Sony's PS5 page carries a notice that from January 2028 'newly released games on PlayStation will be available for purchase on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital format only', and Sony's terms say a Store purchase is a personal licence that is not transferable.

economical.note: PlayStation Direct listed the 1TB PS5 at $649.00 when checked. Online multiplayer is a PlayStation Plus benefit; the cheapest tier, Essential, is $79.99 a year, so year one costs about $729.

products.name: PlayStation 5 Digital Edition
products.description: The PS5 without a disc drive: every game is a licence on a Sony account unless you buy the add-on drive.

repairability.note: The Digital Edition belongs to the same slim model group as the disc PS5 (Sony lists it as CFI-2000). iFixit's device page lists the same replacement guides, and it has no current numeric score; Sony sells no repair parts.

longevity.note: Plays the same PS4 back catalogue as the disc model, but Sony notes 'PS4 game discs can't be used with the PlayStation®5 Digital Edition' unless an add-on drive is fitted.

ownership.note: Sony's terms say 'you buy a personal license to use that product for private, non-commercial use', not transferable unless local law requires. With no drive, nothing can be resold; Sony's optional add-on disc drive needs an internet connection to pair.

economical.note: PlayStation Direct listed the Digital Edition at $599.00; adding PlayStation Plus Essential at $79.99 a year for online play gives about $679 in year one.

products.name: PlayStation 5 Pro
products.description: Sony's most powerful console, sold without a disc drive, and the most expensive home console here.

repairability.note: iFixit's device page for the PS5 Pro lists replacement guides including an easy-access CMOS battery behind one screw, its fan and power supply; iFixit's 2024 teardown called the gains incremental and criticised tamper-evident warranty stickers. No numeric score and no Sony parts.

longevity.note: Same PS4 backward compatibility as other PS5 models, with no PS3 disc support, according to Sony's support page.

ownership.note: Sold as an all-digital 2TB console; games bought on PlayStation Store are licences under Sony's terms, and Sony says new games go digital-only from January 2028.

economical.note: PlayStation Direct listed the PS5 Pro 2TB at $899.00, marked currently unavailable, when checked; with PlayStation Plus Essential ($79.99 a year) the first year is about $979.

products.name: Xbox Series X (disc, 1TB)
products.description: Microsoft's flagship console with a disc drive and the widest back catalogue of any home console.

repairability.note: iFixit's Xbox Series X device page shows 7 out of 10 from its teardown, and iFixit's store lists Series X replacement parts such as the power supply and heat sink.

longevity.note: Xbox's backward compatibility page says you can 'Play thousands of Original XBOX, XBOX 360, and XBOX One games' on Series X.

ownership.note: The disc model plays physical games; digital purchases are, in Microsoft's Store terms, 'licensed, not sold, to you'.

economical.note: Xbox's page listed the 1TB Disc Drive Series X at $799.99. Online console multiplayer is part of Game Pass Essential at $9.99 a month, so year one comes to about $920.

products.name: Xbox Series X All-Digital
products.description: The Series X without a disc drive, so every game is a Microsoft account licence.

repairability.note: Same Series X platform that iFixit scored 7 out of 10 (its teardown was of the disc model); iFixit's store sells Series X replacement parts such as the power supply.

longevity.note: Plays backward-compatible Xbox One, Xbox 360 and original Xbox games bought digitally; without a drive, older discs you own cannot be used.

ownership.note: Digital only: Microsoft's Store terms say software and digital content 'is licensed, not sold, to you', so nothing bought for it can be resold.

economical.note: Xbox's page listed the 1TB All-Digital Series X at $749.99; with Game Pass Essential for online play ($9.99 a month) year one is about $870.

repairability.note: iFixit has no score for the Series S, but its parts store lists parts marked Genuine Microsoft Part for the Series S, such as the Bluetooth board and HDMI port, alongside a fan assembly and power supply: a better supply than Sony or Nintendo offer.

longevity.note: Xbox's backward compatibility page notes Series S is for 'digital games only', but most Xbox One games and selected Xbox 360 and original Xbox games play on it.

ownership.note: All-digital: games are Microsoft Store licences, which the Store terms say are licensed, not sold.

economical.note: Xbox's page listed the 512GB Series S at $499.99; with Game Pass Essential at $9.99 a month, about $620 in year one.

products.name: Nintendo Switch 2
products.description: Nintendo's 2025 hybrid console, which plays most Switch games but scored 3 out of 10 for repair.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table scores the Switch 2 3 out of 10: the battery and display are glued and the charge ports soldered, and 'Nintendo has yet to provide any repair instructions or replacement parts.'

longevity.note: Nintendo says Switch 2 'can play compatible physical and digital games that have been released on Nintendo Switch', though some may not be supported or fully compatible.

ownership.note: Regular game cards hold the full game, but Nintendo's support page explains that game-key cards hold no game data and act as a key to download it over the internet. Digital purchases are licensed, not sold, under Nintendo's terms.

economical.note: Nintendo's store listed the Switch 2 system at $499.99; Nintendo Switch Online for online play is $19.99 a year, so about $520 in year one.

products.name: Nintendo Switch OLED Model
products.description: The 2021 OLED version of the original Switch, still sold, whose library carries over to Switch 2.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table scores the Switch OLED 4 out of 10: 'Strong adhesives hamper battery and display repairs', and Nintendo offers no repair parts or instructions.

longevity.note: The Switch OLED plays only Switch games, but those games carry forward: Nintendo's transfer guide says Switch 2 plays compatible Switch games and lets you move save data.

ownership.note: Switch game cards contain the full game and can be lent or resold; Nintendo's game-key card page contrasts them with Switch 2 key cards, which do not contain the full game data. Digital games are licences under Nintendo's purchase terms.

economical.note: Nintendo's store listed the OLED Model at $399.99; with Nintendo Switch Online at $19.99 a year, about $420 in year one.

products.name: Nintendo Switch
products.description: The original 2017 Switch, still on sale, now scored 4 out of 10 by iFixit after a rescoring.

repairability.note: iFixit cut the original Switch from 8 to 4 out of 10 in 2025, explaining that 'Nintendo has never made any replacement parts publicly available' and the battery is still glued.

longevity.note: Its games play on Switch 2, which Nintendo says runs compatible Switch games and accepts transferred save data, so a library bought now is not stranded.

ownership.note: Uses the same full-game cartridges as the OLED Model; Nintendo's purchase terms say digital software is licensed, not sold.

economical.note: Nintendo's store listed the Switch at $339.99; with Nintendo Switch Online ($19.99 a year), about $360 in year one.

products.name: Nintendo Switch Lite
products.description: The handheld-only Switch, cheapest of Nintendo's line, and the hardest of them to repair.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table scores the Switch Lite 3 out of 10; strong adhesives hamper battery and display repairs, the USB-C port is soldered and Nintendo offers no parts.

longevity.note: Plays the Switch library, which Nintendo's transfer guide says carries forward to Switch 2.

ownership.note: Takes the same full-game Switch cartridges; Nintendo's game-key card explainer confirms regular game cards contain the full game data.

economical.note: Nintendo's store listed the Switch Lite at $229.99; adding Nintendo Switch Online at $19.99 a year gives about $250 in year one, the cheapest mainstream console here.

products.name: Steam Deck OLED
products.description: Valve's handheld PC running SteamOS, with official parts through iFixit and the whole Steam back catalogue.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table scores the Steam Deck OLED 7 out of 10 and says 'Valve offers original replacement parts and repair instructions for end users', though the battery is strongly glued. Valve's FAQ points owners to iFixit for parts and guides.

longevity.note: A PC: Valve's FAQ says your Steam library shows up once you log in, non-Steam games can run through Proton, and installed games play offline unless the game itself needs a connection.

ownership.note: Steam's Subscriber Agreement says 'The Content and Services are licensed, not sold', so a Steam library cannot be resold; the Deck can also run non-Steam games, including copies bought without DRM elsewhere.

economical.note: Steam's store listed the 512GB OLED at $789.00 (1TB at $949.00). Valve charges no subscription for online play.

products.name: Steam Deck LCD (Valve Certified Refurbished)
products.description: The original LCD Steam Deck, now sold by Valve only as a tested refurbished unit with a one-year warranty.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table scores the Steam Deck (LCD) 7 out of 10, with modular parts and M.2 storage but a strongly glued battery; Valve parts are sold through iFixit.

longevity.note: Runs the same SteamOS and Steam library as the OLED model, on an older, less efficient chip; Valve's FAQ covers both models.

ownership.note: Steam games are licences under the Subscriber Agreement, which says they confer 'no title or ownership'.

economical.note: Valve's refurbished store listed the 256GB LCD at $319.00 (64GB $279.00), out of stock on the day checked; refurbished stock comes and goes.

products.name: Steam Machine
products.description: Valve's 2026 living-room PC running SteamOS, sold through a waitlist when checked.

repairability.note: iFixit has not scored it. Its Steam Machine (2026) device page lists OEM replacement guides for parts from the fan and power supply to the motherboard, RAM and SSD, and says it was released in June 2026; it has no battery to glue. This is a different kind of evidence from a score.

longevity.note: Valve says it plays your whole Steam library and runs SteamOS 3; as a PC it also runs games from other sources.

ownership.note: Games bought on Steam are licences, not sales, under the Steam Subscriber Agreement.

economical.note: Valve's page lists the 512GB model at $1,049 (2TB at $1,349) and invites buyers to join a waitlist; no subscription for online play.

products.name: ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X
products.description: ASUS and Microsoft's high-end Windows handheld, with iFixit's 7 out of 10 and ASUS-supplied parts.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table gives the ROG Xbox Ally X a provisional 7 out of 10: the battery, thumbsticks, fan and storage are modular, and 'Asus provides a good selection of repair parts and instructions'; the charge port and most buttons are soldered.

longevity.note: Runs Windows 11, so ASUS says it reaches your full library of PC games from Xbox and other game stores; PC games bought decades ago still run.

ownership.note: Microsoft Store and Xbox PC purchases are licensed, not sold, but as a Windows PC it also runs games from stores that sell copies without DRM.

economical.note: ASUS's US eShop listed the ROG Xbox Ally X at $999.99 when checked; Game Pass is optional.

products.name: ASUS ROG Xbox Ally
products.description: The cheaper Ally model with a less powerful chip; iFixit has not scored it.

longevity.note: ASUS's product page says it is powered by Windows 11 and gives access to your full library of PC games from Xbox and other game stores.

ownership.note: Same licence terms as any Microsoft Store purchase (licensed, not sold), with the option of other PC stores.

economical.note: ASUS's US eShop listed the ROG Xbox Ally (16GB, 512GB) at $599.99.

products.name: Retroid Pocket 5
products.description: A small-maker Android handheld built for retro gaming, with an OLED screen and a 6 out of 10 iFixit score.

repairability.note: iFixit's handheld table gives the Retroid Pocket 5 6 out of 10: battery, thumbsticks and fan are straightforward to replace, but storage and charge port are soldered and 'Retroid does not provide repair parts or instructions.'

longevity.note: Retroid's store page lists Android 13 with official over-the-air updates; Android apps and emulators run, but the device depends on a small maker's update support.

ownership.note: An open Android device with no first-party game store: what you can play depends on the apps you install and games you own, rather than a console maker's licence system.

economical.note: Retroid's store listed the Retroid Pocket 5 at $209.00 regular price ($179.00 on sale when checked); no subscription.

products.name: Playdate
products.description: Panic's tiny crank-controlled handheld with its own indie game catalogue and easy sideloading.

repairability.note: iFixit's Playdate device page shows 6 out of 10 from its teardown.

longevity.note: Plays only Playdate games: the bundled Season and Panic's Catalog store plus homemade games. A small, single-platform library, though Panic's free SDK keeps new games coming.

ownership.note: Panic says 'sideloading games onto the Playdate is easy' and its SDK is free, so games can be loaded without going through Panic's store; the price includes a full Season of 24 games.

economical.note: Panic's site lists the Playdate at $229 plus taxes and shipping, with no subscription.

products.name: Analogue Pocket
products.description: A handheld that plays original Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges, with adapters for other systems.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. iFixit's Analogue Pocket device page lists community replacement guides for the battery, screen, shells, speakers and main board, and Analogue's Pocket FAQ says battery replacements go through Analogue Support and Analogue Repair; Analogue does not sell parts to owners.

longevity.note: Analogue says Pocket is compatible out of the box with the 2,780+ Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridge library, plus Game Gear, Neo Geo Pocket and TurboGrafx-16 cards with adapters.

ownership.note: Plays physical cartridges you own with no account or internet; Analogue states 'Analogue Pocket does not play copyrighted rom files, it plays legacy game cartridges via the cartridge slot.'

economical.note: Analogue's store listed the Pocket at $239.99 on preorder when checked; cartridges are bought separately, often second-hand.
